source.title: Comparing Sparsified MLPs and Transcoders: Many Transcoder Features Are Neurons in Disguise

record.tranche_reason: The study measures neuron interpretability and activation clusters in language models using sort evaluations and case studies, rather than reproducing the original vision-neuron examples.
record.gate_note: The study directly compares neuron interpretability across activation-range sampling conditions and examines a polysemantic-neuron case. Cited findings from prior work and results on transcoder training, reconstruction, and arithmetic are not rows unless they directly measure the claim’s neuron behavior.
record.test_reason: The study argues that sign-split, top-k-thresholded MLP neurons are more monosemantic than commonly assumed, which bears on V2. In Gemma 3 4B L22 sort evals, neurons' top activations score comparably to transcoder features, while quantile sampling degrades neuron scores. The authors explicitly restate polysemanticity as a property of broad activation ranges. A single-neuron case study (N5039+) shows distinct activation clusters. T5 fits better than T2 because the paper's own results argue the common-LM-polysemanticity version needs restating.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that neuron features account for a substantial share (often over half) of transcoder activations in late layers. These features carry nearly all Jacobian faithfulness and recur across seeds, so sign-split, top-k neurons are a stronger interpretability basis than commonly assumed. Neurons' top activations are about as monosemantic as transcoder features, while broad activation ranges are polysemantic. The 'red' case is preliminary evidence of real polysemanticity that transcoders resolve by recombining a few neurons. They note they characterise only sparse, high-magnitude activations.
record.recipe_differences: Uses sign-split neuron activations, transcoder comparisons, sort evaluations, and a targeted activation-cluster case study; it does not reproduce the original vision-neuron procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: Sort-evaluation outcome depends on activation sampling: peak-only contexts yield neuron scores comparable to transcoder features, while quantile sampling yields noticeably worse neuron scores.

fits_no_version.finding: In student-teacher distillation of the Gemma 3 4B L17 MLP, narrower GeGLU students represent teacher neurons without matching weights (7% vs 9% matched at N=2560). Single student neurons (e.g. em-dash neuron 2188) push several teacher neurons' directions at once. Teacher activation energy predicts which neurons are kept (AUC 0.73 to 0.94).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Under width compression, student neurons represent multiple teacher neurons in superposition, prioritising high-energy ones.

fits_no_version.finding: Dense-model neurons' best bigram probe feature fires on the target bigram about 0% of the time (Gemmascope 75.6%). Gemma 4 26B-A4B MoE neurons hit 20.1% (Table 7).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Fine-grained concepts such as bigrams are not represented monosemantically by dense MLP neurons; MoE neurons represent them more often.

record.peer_reviewed: 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026), workshop: Interpretability as a Science
record.problems: For the claim-relevant evidence, the sort-evaluation comparison is reported qualitatively in a figure without numerical values or stated uncertainty. Results are limited to Gemma 3 4B for this comparison, and the polysemantic-neuron case is a single preliminary example. The paper states that it runs no systematic human evaluation and relies on automated interpretability metrics.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-relevant neuron polysemanticity outcomes were identified. Other reported evaluations concern reconstruction, replacement, sparse probing, or induced behaviors rather than the versions tested here.

untested.parts: The share of polysemantic neurons is never counted. Layer dependence is only hypothesised (fn. 9: early-layer neurons may be more polysemantic), not measured. Sort evals cover only Gemma 3 4B L22.
No test of whether capacity pressure causes polysemanticity in the studied LMs; the toy student-teacher result is recorded separately.
Polysemantic neurons arising without capacity pressure are not examined; the initialization results concern transcoder features.
No comparison of polysemantic-neuron share across activation functions, architectures or regularization.
How often unrelated mixtures occur across neurons is not estimated. Canonical polysemantic neurons are not re-examined.
Explanation-scoring methods are not varied; only the sampled activation range is varied.

missing.what: Cluster sort eval on 50 random Gemma 3 4B L22 neurons: 16-cluster k-means on each neuron's top 4096 activations gives clusters a judge distinguishes with 0.933 accuracy; transcoder clusterings give 0.79 to 0.94. This is evidence that many neurons' high activations contain distinct sub-concepts, though whether these are unrelated or related offshoots is not determined.
Manual inspection of MoE attribution graphs: shared-expert neurons described as largely polysemantic, with possible polysemanticity within routed experts. This is preliminary and qualitative.

record.verdict_notes: The claim-relevant evidence is thin: one model and layer, figure-only sort-eval values, automated (Claude Haiku) judging, and a single case study. The paper's thrust (neurons more monosemantic than assumed at top activations) weakens V2 as usually stated, which is why the tranche is T5.

versions.untested_parts: No image classifier or InceptionV1 neurons are studied.

The study does not estimate the share of polysemantic neurons across language models or layers; the sort evaluation is reported for Gemma 3 4B, layer 22, and does not directly count neurons responding to unrelated concepts.
The study discusses superposition but does not test whether capacity pressure causes polysemanticity in the studied models.
Initialization and training effects on transcoder features are studied, not whether polysemantic neurons arise without capacity pressure.
The study compares dictionary setups and neuron features, but does not measure how architecture or regularization changes the share of polysemantic neurons or its performance cost.
The study gives a single neuron case study and does not estimate how frequent truly unrelated mixtures are across models.
The study varies activation-range sampling in sort evaluations, but does not systematically vary explanation-scoring methods.

rows.subject: Gemma 3 4B
rows.operation_detail: Compared neuron and transcoder-feature sort-evaluation scores using the highest-activating contexts.
rows.value: Figure only; text says neurons score comparably to transcoder features at the top of the activation distribution.
rows.note: The reported comparison concerns interpretability of peak activations, not the prevalence of polysemantic neurons.
rows.check: Relative to the transcoder baseline, neurons show no interpretability deficit when only the 10 top-activating excerpts are shown (§2.5, Fig. 3b). So V2's polysemanticity is not visible in this regime; state should be absent, not partial. Values are figure-only. Sort-eval accuracy is pairwise discriminability, not a polysemanticity rate. For V7 the evidence is the contrast with R2, not this row alone.

rows.subject: Gemma 3 4B, layer 22, neuron N5039+
rows.operation_detail: Examined the neuron’s high-activation contexts and grouped them by which transcoder feature activated most strongly.
rows.value: The neuron’s activations form distinct clusters described as involving red, transparency/clarity, display, visibility, appearance, and other patterns; two non-neuron features are described as isolating interpretable clusters.
rows.note: The authors present this as preliminary evidence of real polysemanticity in this neuron, while noting the features can combine neurons to yield cleaner concepts.
rows.check: This is a single neuron, so for V2 it shows that polysemantic neurons exist, not that they are a large share. Clusters come from UMAP of the top 4096 activations, coloured by an older k=64 TopK transcoder trained on a different hookpoint (fn. 26), not the sweep transcoders. For V6 the state is effectively absent: better tools resolve the neuron into distinct concepts (red, transparency/fairness, appearance/visibility, display, redirect) rather than one shared feature.

relation.reason: The sort evals and the N5039+ case study bear directly on V2, V6 and V7.

tranche.reason: The paper argues that sign-split, top-k neurons are more monosemantic than commonly assumed and that polysemanticity shows only at broad activation ranges. That is an argument that V2 needs restating. T2 would also be defensible.

source_check.notes: R1 and R2 are figure only, and the baseline is GemmaScope features. The text ties the quantile-sampling degradation to higher neuron TopK k ('higher k'). The N5039+ clusters use an older k=64 TopK transcoder on a different hookpoint, and the authors call the case preliminary. R3's 'observed' state refers to polysemanticity (V2); for V6 it counts against the version. The authors are Anthropic-affiliated.

statements.correction: Sort eval (Lindsey et al. 2024): a Claude Haiku 4.5 judge sees 10 excerpts each for features A and B and classifies a held-out excerpt; 500 trials per configuration; no explanations or descriptions are scored. Gemma 3 4B (pt) L22 findings as stated are correct.
statements.problem: Groups this study under 'scoring by explanation or description', but sort eval scores no explanation; it is a judge discrimination test on example excerpts.
Correct: the text only hypothesises that early-layer neurons are more polysemantic (footnote 9, line 827); it gives no per-layer count of polysemantic neurons.
The Gemma citation matches the text's qualitative statement that neurons are polysemantic at broad activation ranges.
Minor omission: the colouring transcoder is an older k=64 TopK transcoder on a different hookpoint, not the one used in the sweeps. The authors also say the clustering point 'may be debated'.

statements.correction: arXiv:2610.24521 authors: Shabalin (Anthropic Fellows, Georgia Tech) and Piotrowski (Anthropic); work supported by the Anthropic Fellows Program. No author is shared with the SoLU paper, but the institution is the same.
statements.problem: Counts the Gemma result (arXiv:2610.24521) among 'groups other than the original's', but the authors are Anthropic-affiliated, the same lab as the SoLU original.

reader_labels.reason: Broad-range sort scores degrade for neurons relative to transcoder features (R2), and N5039+ has multiple described activation clusters (R3). These results are evidence of mixed neuron responses, but do not establish how common they are.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: Neuron scores are described as comparable to transcoder features when only peak activations are examined, so the conclusion depends on the activation range sampled (R1).

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.reason: The case study reports multiple distinct activation clusters rather than one clearly shared feature for this neuron (R3); it does not establish how frequent such cases are.
